units.sentence: Starting no later than July 1, 2027, public high school students won't be allowed to use, hold or wear phones or similar devices during the school day, including time between classes.
units.evidence_span: Beginning no later than July 1, 2027, no public school student in grades nine through 12 shall be permitted to access personal electronic devices during the school day
units.problem: The date, grades and between-class coverage are correct. But P-003 defines access as viewing, holding, wearing or using a device 'for the purpose of communication, internet access, gaming, recording, listening to music, or any other function commonly associated with personal electronic devices'. Without that purpose clause, the sentence reads as if simply holding or carrying a phone is banned, which conflicts with the storage options in P-009 (locker, locked pouch). It also leaves out P-007's 'except as otherwise provided in this Code section or required by law'.
units.suggested_fix: Starting no later than July 1, 2027, public high school students won't be allowed to access phones or similar devices (use, view, hold or wear them for calls, texts, internet, games, recording, music and similar functions) during the school day, including time between classes.

units.sentence: Some students with health or disability plans that require a device are exempt.
units.evidence_span: shall be permitted to access the device as necessary to fulfill the requirements of the respective program or plan
units.problem: 'Exempt' overstates P-013. These students are not exempt from the ban. They may access the device only 'as necessary to fulfill the requirements' of an IEP, Section 504 Plan or medical plan that 'explicitly mandates' it. In the 30-second summary, a reader could take 'exempt' to mean free phone use.
units.suggested_fix: Students whose IEP, Section 504 plan or medical plan explicitly requires a device may use it, but only as the plan requires.

units.sentence: An Emory public health professor, Julie Gazmararian, said, "Parents’ concerns about emergency access are valid and understandable. However, effective cellphone policies can address this..."
units.evidence_span: effective cellphone policies can address this by establishing rapid parent notification systems and guaranteed access to phones when needed
units.problem: The quote is verbatim. Minor: P-037 calls her a 'professor of epidemiology at the Rollins School of Public Health'. 'Emory' comes from the passage label and source (S12), not the passage text.

units.sentence: The law requires emergency communication to go through school systems run by staff.

units.sentence: The law doesn't require the rapid notification or guaranteed phone access Gazmararian described, though districts can add them because the law sets minimum rules.
units.marker: {analysis: no such requirement in the full enacted text; P-008 says policies must "at a minimum" include its list}
units.problem: The first clause is right. The second goes too far. 'At a minimum' (P-008) lets districts add policy provisions, but P-007 bars student access to personal devices 'except as otherwise provided in this Code section or required by law', and P-011(A) sends 'all emergency communication' through school systems. A district therefore cannot guarantee students access to their own phones in emergencies. It can add rapid parent notification and provide school phones (school equipment, P-017 and P-058). The sentence also conflicts with line 143 ('no emergency exception').
units.suggested_fix: The law doesn't require the rapid notification or guaranteed phone access Gazmararian described. Districts can add faster parent alerts and access to school phones, but the law doesn't let them allow students' own phones in emergencies unless a plan or another law requires it.

units.sentence: Adams's lockdown account is one family's experience; the source doesn't say when it happened or what phone rules applied.
units.problem: Accurate, but similar caveats are not applied to supporters' anecdotal claims, such as Woods's 'nothing but support from teachers' (see framing issues).

framing_issues.text: Who disagrees: Woods told lawmakers he had heard nothing but support from teachers across Georgia.
framing_issues.issue: Uneven caveats. Woods's sweeping anecdotal claim appears twice (lines 81 and 156) with no caveat, even though the same sources quote a teacher (Adams) who opposes the law. Adams's own anecdote gets an explicit 'one family's experience' caveat (line 146). Either caveat both or neither, for example by noting that Woods's statement is his own impression and that Adams, a teacher, voiced concerns.

framing_issues.text: In a Florida study, test scores rose ..., and effects were larger in middle and high schools.
framing_issues.issue: One-sided use of an ambiguous finding. P-040's 'the effects of cellphone bans are more pronounced in middle and high school settings' doesn't say it is limited to the gains; it may also cover the suspension rise (P-039). The document presents it only as a benefit (lines 81 and 107) and as a rebuttal (line 169), never alongside the costs.

framing_issues.text: The Florida study is a 2025 working paper designed to estimate cause and effect.
framing_issues.issue: Uneven methodological caveats between studies. The pro-ban Florida study is described as 'designed to estimate cause and effect' without P-038's 'quasi-experimental' (non-randomized) qualifier. The skeptical English study's limits are stated twice ('at one point in time', 'can show links, not cause and effect').

framing_issues.text: We found no evidence against this claim, and the English study didn't measure test scores.
framing_issues.issue: This empties the 'What challenges it' slot for a pro-law claim on the basis of an abstract's partial outcome list ('Secondary outcomes included...', P-064). The same reasoning is used at line 122 ('didn't measure friendships'). The gap may be real, but the document states it with more certainty than the passages allow, and it favors one side.

framing_issues.text: Who benefits: ... Among parents who back a ban, 87.7% expected ... Sen. Sally Harrell said legislators want to hear teachers say ... Woods told lawmakers ...
framing_issues.issue: Option B's 'Who benefits' mixes one measured outcome (Florida) with expectations (survey reasons), a legislator's aspiration and an anecdote. Under a 'benefits' heading, these read as demonstrated benefits. Consider labeling them 'what supporters expect'.

framing_issues.text: Who pays: Students in districts without limits keep their phones in class.
framing_issues.issue: Calling continued phone access a cost to students adopts the pro-ban premise. Option A also lists the missed Florida gains as a cost but doesn't list avoiding the Florida first-year suspension rise (P-039) as a benefit, while Option B lists that rise as a cost.

framing_issues.text: In the Senate, 13 senators voted for an amendment that would have let districts allow phones between classes.
framing_issues.issue: Missing context. Placed right after the count of supporters and critics, this can read as 13 senators opposing the law. The Senate then passed the bill 52-0 (P-025), so at least 9 of those 13 voted for it. The sentence also drops the amendment's grades 9-12 limit.

framing_issues.text: Among parents who support a ban, 60.3% expected better physical health and safety.
framing_issues.issue: This stretches a survey item. General 'physical health and safety' is offered as a counter to the specific concern about emergency contact.

framing_issues.text: The law requires emergency communication to go through school systems run by staff.
framing_issues.issue: Listing the law's own requirement under 'What challenges it' implies it answers the concern. But the document says there is no data on how such systems perform (lines 141 and 147), and Gazmararian's quote first calls the concern 'valid and understandable'.

framing_issues.text: Among parents who oppose a ban, 26.6% said phones are needed for health tools or apps and 19.8% said they're needed for schoolwork.
framing_issues.issue: These reasons are about need, not maturity, so they don't support the 'old enough to manage' claim. The document also doesn't mention that the law partly addresses both needs (P-013 plan exception, P-017 school-provided laptops and tablets).

framing_issues.text: Some students with health or disability plans that require a device are exempt.
framing_issues.issue: In the most-read section, 'exempt' overstates a limited, as-necessary permission (P-013), which could mislead families about what students with plans may do.

framing_issues.text: Also new in this law: Districts must set rules for off-campus activities like field trips, school transportation and sports.
framing_issues.issue: This pre-existing requirement (P-065) is listed under 'Also new in this law', which suggests the requirement itself is new.

framing_issues.text: The law gives schools state guidance but sets aside no money
framing_issues.issue: Policy acts rarely appropriate funds; that happens in budget acts, which were not reviewed. Without that context, readers may infer there is no state funding at all.

framing_issues.text: Woods called for extending the ban ...
framing_issues.issue: Woods is referred to by surname at lines 74 and 81 before he is identified as State School Superintendent Richard Woods (line 106). Readers of Layer 3 can't tell who he is or what his role is.
